Hamer 2007 Study characteristics Methods A randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled superiority trial Participants 456 HIV‐seropositive pregnant women in 3 district health clinics in Zambia Inclusion criteria HIV‐1 infection All gravidities Gestation of 16 to 28 weeks Free of an acute illness requiring hospitalization Willing to deliver at a study maternity clinic Exclusion criteria Age < 18 years Prior enrolment in this study Residence outside of or intent to move out of the catchment areas of the clinics Severe anaemia (haemoglobin level < 6 g/dL) History of allergic reactions to sulfa drugs Prior major pregnancy complications (e.g. breech presentation, severe pre‐eclampsia, ≥ 2 caesarean sections) Major illness likely to influence pregnancy outcomes Interventions Monthly SP for IPTp vs 2‐dose SP for IPTp (standard of care) Outcomes The primary outcomes of this study were the prevalence of placental malaria infection and the prevalence of maternal peripheral parasitaemia at delivery. The differences between protocol and review listed in this section are in reference to the revised protocol on PROSPERO ( CRD42021233901 ). Types of participants After screening the potential studies for inclusion in the review, we decided to revise our inclusion criteria to read that we would accept studies from areas of 'stable' rather than 'moderate‐to‐high' malaria transmission. IPTp has traditionally been recommended in countries with moderate to high malaria transmission (also named “stable” transmission areas, characterized by a steady prevalence pattern, with little variation from one year to another) and not in low transmission settings. That is the reason why in many IPTp studies the malaria transmission intensity is mentioned. Since June 2022, WHO chemoprevention recommendations (including IPTp) no longer specify transmission intensity thresholds to provide greater flexibility to national malaria programmes to adapt control strategies to suit their settings. We edited the wording of the review to reflect this updated recommendation. Types of outcomes We changed our outcome 'small for gestational age' from a primary to a secondary outcome. We added 'severe anaemia' as a secondary outcome. We edited the "severe adverse events" subcategory of outcomes and included "serious adverse events" as outcome. These were analysed as reported in the included studies. We revised and modified the order of the primary and secondary outcomes in the Methods section to organize them in a more intuitive and understandable way. When a study evaluated our outcomes in ways other than we had specified in our Methods, we presented that data. We performed the analyses using the data extracted from the included studies. We presented some outcomes as dichotomous (e.g. low birth weight, undetectable viral load), even if as had planned to present them as continuous. Similarly, we reported the outcomes of interest as defined and assessed in the original studies. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses We did not conduct subgroup analyses based on gravidity, CD4 counts, or malaria transmission for the primary outcomes due to small sample size and unavailability of disaggregated data. We did not conduct subgroup analyses based on use of LLINs as these were used in the trials or data on LLINs were not available. We did not conduct sensitivity analysis since not all trials reported in detail the proportion of missing data and the reasons for all exclusions in the evaluation of each individual outcome. It was not possible to conduct sensitivity analysis consistently across all comparisons. GRADE and summary of findings tables We added a section on assessing the certainty of the evidence and creating summary of findings tables for the comparisons and outcomes that we considered to be the most important for those making decisions about malaria prevention for HIV‐positive pregnant women. We had not specified in the protocol which comparisons and outcomes we would include in summary of findings tables. We chose our meta‐analysis of studies evaluating the current standard of care (daily cotrimoxazole) compared to IPTp (mefloquine or dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine) as our main comparison for our first summary of findings table, omitting drug‐related adverse events and HIV mother‐to‐child transmission, as we considered these to be drug‐specific. In a second summary of findings table, we chose to present results for dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine plus daily cotrimoxazole versus daily cotrimoxazle alone as we wanted to focus on the drug that we judged to be the most promising candidate for IPTp in this population. Following Cochrane handbook, we did not include more than eight outcomes in SoF 2, so we omitted two outcomes that were presented in SoF 1 (severe adverse events and cord blood parasitaemia), but these results are available in the main text of the review, as are the results of the mefloquine studies. documents.title: HIV and cardiovascular diseases: a systematic review and comparative risk assessment study.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: People living with HIV (PLWH) face a significantly elevated risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). This study aims to quantify temporal trends in HIV-attributable CVD burden at global, regional and national levels using a comparative risk assessment framework.
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase and MEDLINE for cohort studies from inception to 28 October 2024, assessing HIV infection and CVD risk. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) for total and subtype-specific CVDs were estimated using random-effects meta-analysis. Based on pooled RRs and HIV prevalence data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study, we calculated population attributable fractions (PAFs) from 1990 to 2011. These PAFs were applied to GBD disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) to estimate the age-standardised DALYs rate (ASDRs) of CVDs attributable to HIV by sex, region and year between 2000 and 2021.
FINDINGS: 35 cohort studies with 199 effect estimates were included. HIV infection was associated with increased risk of total CVDs (RR=1.38), stroke (1.90), ischaemic stroke (1.31), haemorrhagic stroke (2.04), ischaemic heart disease (1.72), myocardial infarction (1.60), heart failure (1.71), peripheral vascular disease (1.19) and cardiac arrest (2.58). Subgroup analyses showed higher ischaemic stroke risk in females and increased CVD risk among PLWH with low CD4+ or high viral load. From 1990 to 2011, the global PAF for total CVDs attributable to HIV rose from 0.0814% to 0.2244%. Global ASDR attributable to HIV nearly tripled, increasing from 3.45 to 9.26 per 100 000 population between 2000 and 2021, with stroke and ischaemic heart disease contributing most. The burden was highest in low-Sociodemographic Index regions, particularly southern Africa; in 2021, Lesotho and Eswatini had the highest ASDRs.
INTERPRETATION: HIV-attributable CVD burden has risen substantially over the past two decades, with marked concentration in the African Region. Integrating CVD screening and management into HIV care is urgently needed in high-prevalence settings.

Yet, global evidence on HIV-attributable CVD burden across different regions and subtypes remains limited. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This study provides comprehensive estimates of HIV-related risks for major CVD outcomes and quantifies global, regional and national burdens. We found substantially increased CVD risks among PLWH and a threefold increase in HIV-attributable CVD burden from 2000 to 2021, mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY Our findings highlight the urgent need to integrate CVD prevention and management into HIV care programmes, especially in high-risk countries. The study provides an updated evidence base for guiding resource allocation and global health policy on dual HIV-CVD epidemics. Introduction Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally. 1 Over the past three decades, the burden of CVDs has increased substantially, driven by population ageing, changing lifestyle patterns and the rising prevalence of metabolic and behavioural risk factors. 2 3 In parallel, advances in combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) and its widespread availability have transformed HIV infection from a fatal illness into a chronic, manageable condition, resulting in substantial gains in survival and life expectancy for people living with HIV (PLWH). 4 5 As acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS)-related mortality has declined, the clinical profile of HIV has broadened, with non-communicable diseases, particularly CVDs, now contributing an increasing share of morbidity and mortality among PLWH. 6 Numerous epidemiological studies have shown that PLWH experience a substantially elevated risk of CVD events, including myocardial infarction, stroke and heart failure, compared with individuals without HIV, even after achieving sustained viral suppression. 7–9 In some cohorts, HIV infection has also been associated with increased risks of peripheral vascular disease and aortic aneurysm. 10 11 Notably, CVDs now account for an estimated 4.6% of all deaths among PLWH globally, and more than 5% of deaths in Asian cohorts. 12 13 This elevated risk reflects a multifactorial interplay between chronic immune activation, systemic inflammation and ART-related metabolic effect. 14 HIV is known to promote endothelial dysfunction and arterial inflammation, while several ART regimens, particularly older-generation protease inhibitors and thymidine analogues, have been implicated in dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance and lipodystrophy. 6 15 Histopathological and imaging studies have provided further evidence of early vascular ageing, subclinical atherosclerosis and myocardial remodelling in PLWH, even in the absence of overt clinical disease. 16 17 However, the modifying effects of immune status, viral load and ART exposure on cardiovascular risk remain inconsistent and need further comprehensive exploration. Despite the growing recognition of these risks, global estimates of HIV-attributable CVD burden remain limited. Most existing studies have focused on a narrow range of outcomes, primarily myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke, and have been conducted in high-income settings, limiting their generalisability to low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), where nearly 80% of PLWH reside. 9 18 19 In one of the few global assessments to date, a 2018 study estimated that HIV contributed to 2.6 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) of CVDs, with the highest burden observed in sub-Saharan Africa and the Asia-Pacific region. 7 However, that study did not provide stratified estimates by Sociodemographic Index (SDI), nor did it incorporate more recent epidemiological evidence or the full spectrum of cardiovascular outcomes now recognised to be associated with HIV. Comprehensive and up-to-date estimates of HIV-attributable CVD burden are needed to inform the integration of cardiovascular care into chronic HIV management, particularly in regions with high dual burdens of HIV and CVDs. In this study, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the risk ratios (RRs) of major cardiovascular outcomes associated with HIV infection. We then applied a comparative risk assessment framework using data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 study to estimate the global, regional and national burden of HIV-attributable CVDs. Specifically, we aimed to: (1) quantify the RRs of major CVD outcomes in PLWH compared with HIV-negative individuals; (2) estimate the population attributable fraction (PAF) of CVDs attributable to HIV, stratified by sex, SDI quintile, WHO region and country between 1990 and 2011; and (3) assess temporal trends in age-standardised DALY rates (ASDRs) for HIV-attributable CVDs at global, regional and national levels from 2000 to 2021. Methods Study design and analytic framework We conducted a comparative risk assessment to estimate the global burden of CVDs attributable to HIV infection. The analysis was based on three sequential steps ( figure 1 ). First, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify the RRs of CVD outcomes in PLWH compared with HIV-negative individuals, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines. 20 21 The study protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (registration number: CRD420251069714); Second, we estimated PAFs for HIV-associated CVD outcomes by combining the pooled RRs from the meta-analysis with HIV prevalence data obtained from the GBD 2021 study for the period 1990–2011. Third, we applied a 10-year exposure-outcome lag, consistent with prior GBD comparative risk assessments and the follow-up durations reported in previous HIV-CVD cohort studies, 22–24 to reflect the delayed effects of chronic HIV infection on cardiovascular pathogenesis, whereby prolonged immune activation and endothelial dysfunction accumulate over several years before clinically manifest CVD outcomes. 25 The resulting PAFs were then applied to GBD estimates of CVD DALYs to derive HIV-attributable ASDRs from 2000 to 2021, disaggregated by sex, SDI quintile, WHO region and country. Figure 1 Conceptual framework of global burden of CVDs attributable to HIV. ASDR, age-standardised disability-adjusted life-years rate. Systematic review and meta-analysis Search strategy and selection criteria Our literature identification comprised two steps: (1) an updated electronic database search and (2) a manual screening of reference lists from relevant prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Several systematic reviews and meta-analyses have previously examined the association between HIV infection and incident CVDs. We first reviewed the search periods of these prior studies and identified that while some recent reviews extended beyond 2020 and others ended earlier, most CVD outcomes had already been well covered by studies up to 2020. 26–34 Building on this, we conducted an updated and comprehensive literature search in PubMed, Embase and MEDLINE to identify cohort studies published between 1 January 2020 and 28 October 2024 that investigated the associations between HIV infection and the risk of CVDs. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms related to HIV (eg, “HIV”, “AIDS”, “human immunodeficiency virus”) and CVDs (eg, “cardiovascular disease”, “myocardial infarction”, “stroke”, “heart failure”). No restrictions were applied regarding language or geographic region. Eligible studies were restricted to full-text, peer-reviewed journal articles. To ensure completeness, we also manually screened the reference lists of included articles and relevant prior reviews. The full search strategy is provided in online supplemental table S1 . 10.1136/bmjgh-2025-022324.supp1 Supplementary data Studies were eligible for inclusion if they: (1) used a cohort design; (2) reported the association between HIV infection and the risk of CVD morbidity or mortality; and (3) provided effect estimates as RRs, HRs or ORs with 95% CIs. Eligible CVD outcomes included both composite and specific endpoints, including stroke, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, cerebral aneurysm, ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, cardiac arrest, aortic aneurysm, peripheral vascular disease, sudden cardiac death, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension and coronary heart disease. When multiple publications reported findings from the same cohort population, the one with the most comprehensive data or the largest sample size was retained. However, if distinct CVD subtypes were reported across publications from the same cohort, each was included. We excluded studies that focused solely on individuals with pre-existing CVDs or on CVD-related rehospitalisation, as well as those without a clearly defined HIV exposure group. Screening, data extraction and quality assessment Two reviewers (ZL and CZ) independently screened the titles and abstracts of all retrieved articles, followed by full-text screening of potentially eligible studies. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. Data extraction was independently performed by two investigators (TH and RL) using a predefined and standardised data collection form, and verified by a third investigator (ZL) to ensure accuracy and consistency. The extracted information included: title, first author, publication year, investigation year, study location, WHO region (African Region (AFR), Region of the Americas (AMR), South-East Asian Region (SEAR), European Region (EUR), Eastern Mediterranean Region (EMR) and Western Pacific Region (WPR)), SDI region (high, high-middle, middle, low-middle and low, classified according to the study-year SDI values based on the reference quantiles defined in GBD 2021), sample sources (community-based, health facility-based or combined), sample size, proportion of female participants, participant age (range, mean or median), measurement of HIV, measurement of CVDs and its subtypes, risk estimates (RR, HR or OR), and corresponding 95% CIs, prioritising fully adjusted estimates when multiple models were reported. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), which assigns a maximum of nine stars across three domains: selection of participants, comparability of study groups and ascertainment of outcomes/exposures. 35 Studies were categorised as having good quality (NOS score ≥7), fair quality (score 4–6) or poor quality (score <4). Quality assessment was independently conducted by two reviewers (ZL and TH), with disagreements resolved by consensus. Data sources for HIV prevalence and cardiovascular burden Data on HIV prevalence and DALYs for CVDs were obtained from the GBD 2021 study, coordinated by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation. 36 HIV prevalence was extracted for the period 1990–2011. With a 10-year exposure-outcome lag, DALYs were extracted for the period 2000–2021, for both overall CVDs and six CVD subtypes defined in the GBD database, namely ischaemic heart disease, stroke, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension. Given that most cohorts included individuals aged 18 years and older, the data were extracted by 5-year age intervals (from 20 to 24 to 95+ years). These data were also stratified by sex, SDI region, WHO region and country. Statistical analysis Meta-analysis of effect estimates Included studies reported effect estimates in the forms of HRs, RRs and ORs, along with their 95% CIs. Given the low incidence of CVD events (<5%) among HIV-negative comparator groups in most cohorts, RRs and HRs were considered numerically equivalent and were pooled directly. 37 38 For studies reporting ORs, we applied a standard transformation to approximate RRs 39 using the following formula: R R i j = O R i j 1 - P i + ( P i × O R i j ) S E l n ⁡ ( R R i j ) = S E l n ⁡ ( O R i j ) = l n ⁡ ( U C i j ) - l n ⁡ ( L C i j ) 3 . 92 R R 95 % C I , i j = e l n ⁡ ( R R i j ) ± 1.96 × S E l n ⁡ ( R R i j ) where O R i j is the point estimate of OR from each study i and data point j; R R i j is the point estimate of RR from each study i and data point j; P i is the study-specific prevalence of outcome among the unexposed group (when not reported, prevalence was obtained from previously published meta-analyses of the corresponding outcome); l n is natural log; S E is standard error; L C i j is lower confidence limit and U C i j is upper confidence limit of 95% CI. We conducted a random-effects meta-analysis with the restricted maximum likelihood estimator to calculate pooled effect estimates for overall CVDs and individual subtypes, where at least two studies were available. When multiple subgroup-specific estimates (eg, for sex) were reported within the same study, they were first meta-analysed using a fixed-effects model to generate a single study-level estimate prior to pooling. 40 Pooled RRs with corresponding 95% CIs were reported. Between-study heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic, with values >50% indicating substantial heterogeneity. 41 Publication bias was evaluated through visual inspection of funnel plots, and asymmetry was tested using Egger’s regression test when at least ten estimates were available (a p<0.05 from Egger’s regression test was considered suggestive of small-study effects). 42 Robustness of pooled estimates was explored using leave-one-out sensitivity analyses. Prespecified subgroup analyses were performed by sex (female vs male), age (<50 vs ≥50 years), sex and age (female, younger (<50 years) vs female, older (≥50 years) vs male, younger (<50 years) vs male, older (≥50 years)), ethnicity (white vs non-white), CD4+cell count (<200 vs 200–499 vs ≥500 cells/mm³), HIV viral load (≥500 vs <500 copies/mL), sampling source (community-based vs health facility-based vs combined), and WHO region (AMR vs EUR vs WPR). Credibility and grading of evidence Each pooled estimate was assessed for credibility by two investigators (ZL and TH) using a five-grade classification system based on the strength and consistency of the evidence. Criteria included statistical significance (p value), 95% CI width, between-study heterogeneity (I²), prediction intervals, small-study effects, excess significance bias and whether the largest contributing study reported a significant effect. Based on these dimensions, evidence was classified as convincing (class I), highly suggestive (class II), suggestive (class III), weak (class IV) or non-significant (class NS), as detailed in online supplemental table S2 . 43 44 Additionally, we assessed the quality of evidence for each pooled estimate using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach, categorising them as ‘high’, ‘moderate’, ‘low’ or ‘very low’. 45 According to the GRADE approach, observational studies are initially rated as low-quality evidence. Confidence in the effect estimates may be downgraded based on five criteria: risk of bias, inconsistency among studies, indirectness of the evidence, imprecision and potential publication bias. Conversely, confidence may be upgraded if certain conditions are met, including a large effect size unlikely to be explained by confounders, evidence of a dose-response relationship and no plausible residual confounding that could alter the interpretation of the exposure’s effect. Estimation of HIV-attributable cardiovascular burden To quantify the burden of CVDs attributable to HIV infection, we first calculated the PAF for each outcome using the formula: P A F = P × ( R R - 1 ) P × ( R R - 1 ) + 1 where P is the HIV prevalence and R R is the overall pooled RR for each CVD and its subtype. Estimates were stratified by year, sex, age, WHO region and SDI region. We then applied direct age standardisation using the GBD world standard population as the reference to calculate age-standardised PAFs. 46 To propagate uncertainty, we employed Monte Carlo simulation with 1000 iterations. In each iteration, values were sampled jointly from the beta distribution for HIV prevalence and the log-normal distribution for the pooled RR. The PAF estimates were summarised as the mean and 95% CIs, defined as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the simulated distribution. Next, the HIV-attributable burden of CVDs was then estimated by applying the simulated PAFs to the corresponding DALYs (lagged by 10 years to account for latency between exposure and disease onset) obtained from the GBD 2021 dataset: a t t r i b u t a b l e b u r d e n = P A F × D A L Y s Direct standardisation approach was applied to calculate the ASDRs for individuals aged 20 years and older, using the GBD world standard population as the reference. 46 The same simulation approach was used to propagate uncertainty, generating 1000 estimates of a t t r i b u t a b l e b u r d e n for each stratified group. Final estimates were reported as means with corresponding 95% CIs. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using alternative latency assumptions of 8 and 12 years. For the 8-year lag, PAFs were estimated for 1990–2013 and corresponding ASDRs for 1998–2021, whereas for the 12-year lag, PAFs were estimated for 1990–2009 and corresponding ASDRs for 2002–2021. All statistical analyses were conducted using R, V.4.4.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Statistical tests were two-sided, and p values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Results Study selection and characteristics Based on the reference lists of previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses, we identified 107 records. After excluding 36 irrelevant records, 71 articles underwent full-text assessment. We also identified 8635 bibliographic records through electronic database searches. After removing 349 duplicates and excluding 8178 records based on title and abstract screening, we assessed the full texts of 108 articles. Overall, we assessed 179 full-text articles for eligibility and finally included 35 cohort studies in our systematic review and meta-analysis ( figure 2A ). These studies contributed 199 datapoints on associations between HIV and CVDs. These studies were conducted in five countries: the USA (n=24, 68.57%), Denmark (n=4, 11.43%), China (Taiwan province) (n=3, 8.57%), Canada (n=2, 5.71%) and the UK (n=2, 5.71%) ( figure 2B ). Most included studies were conducted in high SDI regions, with the majority originating from the AMR region (n=26, 74.29%). Of the included studies, 25 were health facility-based (71.43%), nine were community-based (25.71%), and one was conducted in both community and health facility settings (2.86%) ( figure 2C ). The included studies varied substantially in study period (ranging from the mid-1980s to 2020), sample size (from fewer than 2000 to over 18 million participants), and population characteristics. Most studies were published after 2010 (n=33, 94.29%). In terms of effect measures, 28 studies reported HRs (80.00%), six reported RRs (17.14%), and one reported an OR (2.86%). Quality assessment using the NOS criteria indicated that 34 studies (97.14%) were of good methodological quality, while one (2.86%) was of fair quality. Detailed characteristics and quality assessments of the included studies can be found in online supplemental table S3–S5 . Pooled associations between HIV and cardiovascular outcomes As shown in figure 3 , the pooled RR for overall CVDs in PLWH compared with those without HIV was 1.38 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.83; credibility: class IV; GRADE: very low). The associations varied by CVD subtype. For stroke, the pooled RR was 1.90 (95% CI 1.56 to 2.32; class I; low), including both ischaemic stroke (RR=1.31, 95% CI 1.18 to 1.46; class I; low) and haemorrhagic stroke (RR=2.04, 95% CI 1.63 to 2.56; class I; moderate). Significant associations were also found for ischaemic heart disease (RR=1.72, 95% CI 1.40 to 2.13; class II; low), myocardial infarction (RR=1.60, 95% CI 1.36 to 1.87; class II; very low), heart failure (RR=1.71, 95% CI 1.39 to 2.09; class II; very low), peripheral vascular disease (RR=1.19, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.25; class I; low) and cardiac arrest (RR=2.58, 95% CI 2.27 to 2.92; class II; moderate). Among less frequently reported outcomes, increased risks were observed for pulmonary hypertension (RR=1.18, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.34) and atrial fibrillation (RR=1.30, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.70). No statistically significant associations were noted for aortic aneurysm, sudden cardiac death or cerebral aneurysm. The overall certainty of evidence assessed by GRADE ranged from moderate to very low across outcomes, with most estimates rated as low ( online supplemental table S6 ). The funnel plots revealed no evidence of publication bias. Detailed results from the single studies included in the meta-analysis, as well as the forest plot, funnel plot and sensitivity analysis results for each meta-analysis, are provided in online supplemental table S7 . Subgroup analyses revealed several differential patterns in the associations between HIV and CVDs ( online supplemental table S8 ). Subgroup analyses revealed a higher risk of ischaemic stroke in females (RR=1.76, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.52) than in males (RR=1.13, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.28; p for subgroup differences=0.021). No significant sex-based differences were observed for other outcomes. Immunosuppression (CD4+<200 cells/mm³) was strongly associated with increased risk of myocardial infarction (RR=1.83, 95% CI 1.51 to 2.21; p=0.008), heart failure (RR=1.70, 95% CI 1.49 to 1.95; p=0.013), ischaemic stroke (RR=3.20, 95% CI 2.30 to 4.40; p<0.0001), peripheral vascular disease (RR=1.91, 95% CI 1.71 to 2.13; p<0.0001), aortic aneurysm (RR=1.29, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.65; p=0.038), sudden cardiac death (RR=1.57, 95% CI 1.28 to 1.92; p=0.003) and pulmonary hypertension (RR=1.94, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.54; p<0.0001), compared with individuals with preserved immune function (CD4+≥200 cells/mm³). Similarly, high viral load (≥500 copies/mL) was significantly associated with elevated risks of ischaemic stroke (RR=2.24, 95% CI 1.73 to 2.89; p<0.0001), peripheral vascular disease (RR=1.51, 95% CI 1.38 to 1.65; p<0.0001), aortic aneurysm (RR=1.29, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.52; p=0.003), sudden cardiac death (RR=1.70, 95% CI 1.46 to 1.98; p<0.0001) and pulmonary hypertension (RR=1.88, 95% CI 1.46 to 2.42; p=0.0002). For sudden cardiac death, the risk was markedly higher in community-based study (RR=8.15, 95% CI 5.58 to 11.90; p<0.0001) than in health facility-based study, and was also substantially higher in the WPR (RR=8.15, 95% CI 5.58 to 11.90; p<0.0001) compared with the AMR. By sex and age, the higher risks were observed among younger females, for both haemorrhagic stroke (RR=4.32, 95% CI 3.14 to 5.96; p<0.0001) and coronary heart disease (RR=1.31, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.47; p<0.0001). By contrast, no significant subgroup differences were observed across age alone or ethnicity. Burden of CVDs attributable to HIV Global burden of CVDs attributable to HIV Globally, the PAF of HIV-associated CVDs increased from 0.0814% (95% CI 0.0790% to 0.0837%) in 1990 to 0.2244% (0.2201% to 0.2288%) in 2011 ( online supplemental table S9 ). The corresponding ASDR nearly tripled from 3.45 (95% CI 3.42 to 3.48) per 100 000 population in 2000 to 9.26 (95% CI 9.09 to 9.42) in 2021 ( figure 4A and online supplemental table S10 ). The sharpest increase occurred between 2000 and 2010, followed by a period of relative stabilisation from approximately 2010 to 2015, and a subsequent gradual increase thereafter. Among specific CVD subtypes, both the PAFs in 2011 and ASDRs in 2021 were highest for stroke (particularly haemorrhagic stroke) and ischaemic heart disease. In 2011, the global PAFs reached 0.5296% (95% CI 0.5193% to 0.5399%) for stroke and 0.4242% (95% CI 0.4159% to 0.4325%) for ischaemic heart disease, significantly higher than those for ischaemic stroke (0.1832%), atrial fibrillation (0.1773%) and pulmonary hypertension (0.1065%). By 2021, the corresponding ASDRs per 100 000 population were 7.75 (95% CI 7.57 to 7.93) for stroke and 7.94 (95% CI 7.79 to 8.08) for ischaemic heart disease, again markedly surpassing those of other CVDs. Haemorrhagic stroke showed the highest burden among stroke subtypes, with a 2011 PAF of 0.6113% (95% CI 0.5995% to 0.6232%) and a 2021 ASDR of 6.01 (95% CI 5.84 to 6.18) per 100 000 population. In contrast, ASDRs for ischaemic stroke, atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension in 2021 remained low at 0.88, 0.09 and 0.01 per 100 000 population, respectively. Sex-stratified results showed that the relative PAFs were slightly higher in females than in males in 2011, while the ASDR of CVDs attributable to HIV was consistently higher in males (12.70, 95% CI 12.43 to 12.97) than in females (6.35, 95% CI 6.21 to 6.49) in 2021 ( figure 4 , online supplemental table S9, S10 ). Similar trends were observed across CVD subtypes. Regional burden of CVDs attributable to HIV For SDI regions, from 2000 to 2021, ASDR per 100 000 population of HIV-associated CVDs rose from 29.77 (95% CI 29.06 to 30.48) to 41.15 (95% CI 39.80 to 42.49) in low SDI region and from 5.90 (95% CI 5.81 to 5.99) to 17.31 (95% CI 16.91 to 17.72) in low-middle SDI region ( figure 4 , online supplemental table S10 ). By 2021, the ASDR per 100 000 population in low SDI regions remained the highest, particularly for stroke (35.50, 95% CI 34.18 to 36.83), haemorrhagic stroke (29.85, 95% CI 27.99 to 31.71) and ischaemic heart disease (30.43, 95% CI 29.36 to 31.49). Moderate burdens were observed in low-middle SDI and middle SDI regions, while high and high-middle SDI regions reported the lowest ASDRs per 100 000 population of HIV-attributable CVDs at 2.71 (95% CI 2.66 to 2.76) and 2.30 (95% CI 2.25 to 2.35), respectively. These patterns were mirrored in PAFs in 2011, ranging from 0.7028% (95% CI 0.6901% to 0.7154%) in low SDI to 0.0512% (95% CI 0.0464% to 0.0559%) in high-middle SDI ( online supplemental table S9 ). Across WHO regions, a similar divergent trend was observed. The AFR experienced a dramatic rise in ASDR per 100 000 population from 40.68 (95% CI 39.62 to 41.74) in 2000 to 102.18 (95% CI 98.84 to 105.51) in 2021, while most other regions showed either minor increases or stable trends. For example, the ASDR per 100 000 population in SEAR increased from 0.31 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.31) to 4.63 (95% CI 4.53 to 4.74), and AMR from 2.81 (95% CI 2.79 to 2.84) to 5.54 (95% CI 5.45 to 5.63). In contrast, EMR and WPR maintained low levels, reaching only 1.31 (95% CI 1.26 to 1.35) and 1.68 (95% CI 1.60 to 1.75) per 100 000 population, respectively, in 2021. By 2021, AFR remained the most severely affected, with notably high ASDRs per 100 000 population for stroke (99.53 (95% CI 95.91 to 103.14)), haemorrhagic stroke (77.22 (95% CI 72.86 to 81.58)) and ischaemic heart disease (61.51 (95% CI 59.37 to 63.65)). PAFs in 2011 reflected the similar ranking, with AFR reaching 1.7588% (95% CI 1.7381% to 1.7795%) for total CVDs. National burden of CVDs attributable to HIV From 1990 to 2021, national-level HIV-attributable CVD burden demonstrated a clear geographic shift and intensification, particularly in southern Africa ( figure 4 , online supplemental figure S1, S2 ). In 1990, the highest PAFs were observed in Zimbabwe, Uganda, Zambia, Malawi and the United Republic of Tanzania, while by 2000, these countries, especially Uganda, Zimbabwe and Zambia, also ranked among those with the highest ASDRs. However, the epicentre of burden rapidly shifted towards southern Africa in the following decade. By 2011, Eswatini, Lesotho, Botswana, South Africa and Zimbabwe topped the list in PAFs. In 2021, Lesotho, Eswatini, Zimbabwe, Botswana and Zambia reported the highest ASDRs, all exceeding 370 per 100 000 population. Sensitivity analyses using alternative time-lag assumptions (8-year and 12-year lags) showed patterns consistent with the primary 10-year lag analysis ( online supplemental figure S3, table S11 ), with a sustained increasing trend in global ASDRs over time. Across all lag periods, stroke (particularly haemorrhagic stroke) and ischaemic heart disease remained the leading contributors to the HIV-attributable CVD burden, and males consistently exhibited higher ASDRs than females. Discussion Based on 199 effect estimates systematically synthesised from 35 cohort studies, HIV infection was associated with increased risks across multiple CVD outcomes (including total CVDs, stroke, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, cardiac arrest, pulmonary hypertension and atrial fibrillation). The global burden of CVDs attributable to HIV has risen markedly over time. The PAF increased significantly between 1990 and 2011, while the ASDR nearly tripled, from 3.45 to 9.26 per 100 000 population between 2000 and 2021. Among specific CVD types, stroke and ischaemic heart disease contributed most substantially to overall HIV-attributable CVD burden and exhibited the largest increases over time. Marked disparities in burden were observed across sociodemographic strata. The global HIV-attributable CVD burden was higher in males than females and highest in low SDI regions, particularly in the AFR, where the ASDR reached 102.18 per 100 000 population in 2021, far exceeding the global average. These results provide a scientific basis for guiding global and regional public health policy, informing resource allocation and improving clinical management, and highlight the urgent need to integrate CVD prevention and management into comprehensive HIV care strategies. Our study found that PLWH showed significantly increased risks of CVDs. HIV infection was significantly associated with higher risk of CVDs, including total CVDs, stroke, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic heart disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, cardiac arrest, pulmonary hypertension and atrial fibrillation. The pathophysiological mechanisms underlying this association are multifactorial. Persistent immune activation and chronic inflammation represent hallmark features of HIV infection that continue despite effective ART and contribute significantly to CVD risk. 47 The HIV infection process leads to sustained activation of the immune system, characterised by elevated levels of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and high-sensitivity C reactive protein, which contribute to endothelial dysfunction and vascular damage, key precursors to CVDs. 48 49 Moreover, direct damage of HIV proteins on endothelial function and cholesterol metabolism also contributes to cardiovascular pathology. HIV proteins, such as Tat and Nef, accelerate atherosclerosis by damaging endothelial cells and promoting inflammation. 47 The HIV Tat protein can enter dysfunctional endothelial cells via integrin-mediated pathways, promoting viral replication and vascular injury. 50 The HIV Nef protein contributes to cardiovascular pathology by disrupting cholesterol metabolism and impairing reverse cholesterol transport. 51 Besides, microbial translocation from the gut is another contributor to atherosclerosis, further increasing CVD risk. 49 While ART is essential for viral suppression, it has been associated with significant metabolic abnormalities, including dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance and lipodystrophy, all of which compound CVD risk. 47 52 53 The elevated CVD risk among PLWH underscores the urgent need to develop HIV-specific strategies for CVD risk reduction. Beyond viral suppression, an integrated clinical approach, including early cardiovascular risk screening, comprehensive assessment and tailored interventions incorporated into routine HIV care is important. HIV infection was associated with a sex-specific impact on CVD risk, with females exhibiting a significantly higher risk of ischaemic heart disease compared with males. Such a disproportionate risk among females with HIV reflects a confluence of biological vulnerabilities, including reduced oestradiol (E2) levels, metabolic dysregulation and heightened inflammatory responses and immune activation. 54–56 In our study, PLWH with severely depressed immune function of CD4+<200 cells/mm³ and high viral load had significantly increased risk of CVDs. This finding is biologically plausible and supports the central role of uncontrolled viral replication and advanced immunosuppression in driving chronic immune activation, endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis among PLWH, even in the era of ART. 25 57 Furthermore, PLWH in community settings showed high CVD risk. This emphasises social-contextual drivers beyond medical measures in integrated CVD prevention strategies for HIV care delivery. However, we did not observe significant subgroup differences by age or ethnicity. This may be attributable to sample size limitations or underlying data heterogeneity. Future studies with more detailed stratification are warranted to elucidate the potential modifying effects of demographic factors or treatment-related factors on HIV-associated CVD risk. Between 2000 and 2021, the ASDR of CVDs attributable to HIV nearly tripled, with a sharp increase from 2000 to 2010, followed by a period of relative stabilisation from approximately 2010 to 2015, and a subsequent gradual increase thereafter. This trend likely reflects the widespread expansion of ART, which has significantly prolonged life expectancy among PLWH. As PLWH increasingly survive into older age, they become more susceptible to age-related chronic conditions, particularly CVDs, which now represent a growing contributor to long-term morbidity and disability in this population. 53 The most pronounced increases in ASDRs were observed for stroke, particularly haemorrhagic stroke and ischaemic heart disease, substantially exceeding those for atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension and other CVD subtypes. Sex-stratified analyses further revealed distinct patterns between PAF and CVD burden. While PAFs were slightly higher among females than males in 2011, the ASDRs of CVDs attributable to HIV remained consistently higher in males than in females in 2021. This apparent divergence likely reflects differences in baseline cardiovascular risk and background CVD burden between sexes, whereby males generally experience higher absolute CVD rates, while females may exhibit a relatively stronger proportional impact of HIV on cardiovascular risk. 56 58 Together, these findings highlight the increasing importance of sex-specific and disease-specific strategies for cardiovascular prevention and management among ageing PLWH. The ASDR of CVDs attributable to HIV varied greatly across regions and nations, with particularly severe burdens observed in low SDI regions, especially in the AFR. Similarly elevated burdens were seen in low-middle and middle SDI regions. In contrast, high SDI regions exhibited relatively low ASDRs of CVDs attributable to HIV, with the burden showing signs of stabilisation. These disparities likely reflect underlying socioeconomic inequities and weak health systems, which limit access to high-quality healthcare and preventative interventions. 59 60 Regionally, the AFR was most affected, with the ASDR of CVDs attributable to HIV reaching 102.18 per 100 000 in 2021, far higher than the global average. Within AFR, stroke, ischaemic heart disease and haemorrhagic stroke account for the largest shares of the CVD burden attributable to HIV. Similar, though less severe, patterns are evident in the SEAR and AMR regions. Although the burdens in the EMR, EUR and WPR regions remained comparatively lower, recent upward trends suggest the need for continued surveillance and prevention efforts. Shifts in burden rankings at the national level further reflect the evolving influence of epidemic control efforts, economic development and health system performance. These findings have important implications for shaping regional policies, updating clinical guidelines and informing equitable resource allocation. To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive and up-to-date study to systematically evaluate the risk and burden of CVDs, including its main subtypes, among PLWH, using the most recent and comprehensive evidence. Second, this study further explored the association of demographic factors, immune function and viral load with CVD risk among PLWH, highlighting gender differences and HIV-specific mechanisms underlying CVDs in HIV-infected people. Third, this study combined the epidemiological measure PAF and disease burden measure ASDR to complement each other and comprehensively quantify the burden of CVDs attributable to HIV. Fourth, this study revealed the spatial and temporal trends in the burden of CVDs attributable to HIV across different regions from 2000 to 2021, providing valuable insights for targeted public health interventions and resource allocation. This study has several limitations. First, most of the included studies originated from high-income countries, with limited representation from LMICs, potentially limiting the global generalisability of the findings. Second, heterogeneity in study design, follow-up time and covariate adjustment across the included studies may influence the stability and interpretability of the meta-analysis results. Third, although subgroup analyses suggested between-subgroup differences in HIV-associated cardiovascular risks, pooled RRs were applied in the burden estimation to ensure stability and comparability, which may have masked effect modification at finer population levels. Fourth, most studies relied on baseline measurements of immune function and viral load, failing to account for their dynamic nature over time, which may have limited the ability to capture their time-varying effects on cardiovascular risk. Fifth, detailed data on ART regimens, treatment adherence and drug-related adverse effects were lacking, limiting a more detailed understanding of the role of treatment-related factors in cardiovascular risk. In addition, estimates of national and regional disease burden from the GBD study may be subject to systematic bias due to variations in the completeness and quality of medical records and reporting systems. Future research should expand data collection from low-income countries, incorporate more refined analyses of treatment-related factors and validate findings through prospective cohort studies with more detailed subgroup stratification. Conclusions PLWH show increased risks of CVDs and their various subtypes. The burden of CVDs attributable to HIV has grown over time, with the PAF rising significantly between 1990 and 2011, and the ASDR nearly tripling from 2000 to 2021. Substantial regional disparities exist in the global burden of HIV-related CVDs, with the highest burden observed in lower SDI regions, particularly in the AFR. These findings have important policy implications, underscoring the need for tailored cardiovascular risk stratification and treatment strategies within people with HIV, especially in low-income regions where CVDs among PLWH remain highly prevalent. documents.title: Vending machines for reducing harm associated with substance use and use disorders, and co-occurring conditions: a systematic review.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: To stem rising fatal overdoses and other substance use/use disorder (SUD)-related harms, communities are turning to low-barrier harm reduction strategies, such as harm reduction-focused vending machines (VMs) that distribute naloxone, fentanyl test strips, and other harm reduction-related items. This systematic review aims to synthesize literature on VMs for SUD-related harm reduction.
METHODS: Four databases (Embase, Cochrane, PubMed, MEDLINE) were searched from their inception through November 29, 2023. References of identified eligible articles and pertinent prior reviews were also searched for relevant eligible research articles describing VM's feasibility, acceptability, reach, and/or impact when used for SUD-related harm reduction. Data from eligible articles were systematically extracted and summarized.
RESULTS: The search found 45 eligible articles covering 30 separate studies involving 191,242 participants (190,576 VM users; 666 non-users). Most studies were conducted outside of the U.S. (n = 20), focused on individuals who injected drugs (n = 18), and evaluated syringe-dispensing VMs (n = 12). Of the 45 articles, the majority evaluated feasibility (n = 35), followed by acceptability (n = 21), impact (n = 17), and reach (n = 14). The feasibility-assessing articles noted high demand for VM-dispensed items, with usage mostly occurring outside of traditional business hours, and more syringes and HIV self-tests being dispensed compared to some in-person programs. The VMs were generally accepted by target populations, regardless of the items dispensed, and reached high-risk populations. Impact evaluation was limited and based on item dispensed. Seven articles examined the impact of syringe-dispensing VMs and described reductions in syringe sharing (n = 4) and drug use (n = 2), as well as stable or declining rates in drug use-related crime (n = 1). Articles evaluating the impact of HIV self-test-dispensing VMs (n = 3) described HIV detection rates ranging from 1.9% to 17.7%. Two articles reported reduced fatal overdoses after naloxone-dispensing VMs were implemented.
DISCUSSION: VMs show promise as a low-barrier method for reducing SUD-related harm, decreasing health disparities, and engaging hard-to-reach populations. Future implementation science-based research is needed to assess VMs' impact on individual and community health outcomes, including overdose.

Keywords Vending machine Harm reduction Substance use Substance use disorder Addiction HIV prevention Condoms Syringes Dispensing machine Overdose prevention Penn State College of Medicine Department of Family and Community Medicine https://doi.org/10.13039/100006108 National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences KL2 TR002015, UL1 TR002014 pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2025 Background Harms associated with substance use and use disorder (SUD) represent a significant public health threat, with over 100,000 deaths due to drug overdose in the U.S. in 2023 [ 1 ]. Furthermore, the scope of SUD and overdose-related harm has been paralleled by increases in conditions frequently co-occurring with SUD. For example, the rate of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection among people who inject drugs (PWID) increased by 11% from 2016 to 2018, particularly among younger adults [ 2 ]. During the 2019 coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, the U.S. experienced significant increases in fatal overdoses [ 1 , 3 ]. In response to this ongoing crisis, early treatment and prevention strategies aimed at reducing substance use, associated high-risk behaviors (such as higher-risk sexual behaviors), and related harms have been introduced throughout the U.S. However, some people may be unable to access treatment [ 4 ] due to inadequate health plan coverage, lack of health insurance, or stigma [ 5 – 7 ]. In addition, not everyone who use substances may be interested in substance use cessation or reduction [ 8 ]. For those individuals, harm reduction approaches can be beneficial in reducing the harms of substance use and associated higher-risk behaviors, which include HIV, hepatitis C (HCV) and B (HBV) virus infection [ 9 ] or overdose. Examples of harm reduction practices include distribution of naloxone and/or “clean” equipment (e.g., sterile water, cookers, filters), drug checking items (e.g., fentanyl test strips), needle and syringe programs, overdose prevention or supervised consumption sites, and even a provision of opioids (as a safer supply compared to illicitly-obtained opioids) [ 10 – 14 ]. Harm reduction can increase engagement in safer practices, offer a bridge toward treatment, and reduce fatal overdoses [ 15 – 17 ]. In the U.S., many emerging harm reduction strategies [ 18 ], including vending machines (VMs) for naloxone distribution, have been implemented [ 19 – 24 ]. VMs dispensing harm reduction items, mostly sterile needles and syringes, have been present in Europe and Australia since the 1990s [ 14 ]. These early experiences show that these VMs can supplement other harm reduction programs, especially those requiring in-person participation, by offering relative anonymity, reducing stigma associated with in-person attendance, and increasing harm reduction reach within underserved populations and uptake of services due to increased accessibility [ 14 , 25 , 26 ]. For example, VMs can be accessible when traditional services are closed, e.g., during evenings and weekends [ 14 ]. VMs can allow individuals to obtain clean injection supplies who otherwise would be unable to do so, due to limited hours of syringe exchange programs [ 27 ]. As a result, many communities in the U.S. have been increasingly turning to VMs as a means to address harm reduction needs. However, despite VMs’ growing popularity, there is limited research on them as a vehicle for harm reduction, including their impact on health outcomes. Given that VM-delivered harm reduction are increasingly used and represents a promising alternative to traditionally-implemented initiatives, which rely on in-person or face-to-face contact, there is an urgent need to rigorously assess existing evidence on harm reduction-focused VMs and their impact. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review of literature to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, reach, and impact of VMs as an innovative method for delivering SUD-related harm reduction items and services. Methods We followed the PRISMA Extension for Systematic Reviews to conduct this systematic review and summarize its findings [ 28 ]. Eligibility criteria Eligible articles were full-text articles published in English in a peer-reviewed scientific journal that described findings from original research directly examining the feasibility, acceptability, reach, and/or impact of VMs (or similar automated dispensing machines) for SUD-related harm reduction. The eligible article could describe research centered on individuals with SUD, populations with conditions or behaviors frequently co-occurring with substance use or SUD (including higher-risk sexual behaviors), or if the VM-dispensed items were relevant to substance use-related harm reduction. Examples of such VM-dispensed items included, but were not limited to, substance or sexually-transmitted disease (STD) test kits, safer sex supplies, syringes, or sharps disposal. Information sources, search strategy, and selection process A librarian conducted the literature search across four databases (Embase, Cochrane, PubMed, and MEDLINE) from their inception through November 29, 2023, using pre-defined MeSH terms, which are commonly used to index articles in these databases (Table 1 ). References of identified eligible articles and pertinent prior reviews were also reviewed, as were articles solicited from organizations and colleagues whose work focused on SUD-related harm reduction. The entire search process was completed on December 15, 2023 ( Fig. 1 ). The full texts of the remaining, potentially eligible articles were then reviewed by all authors; a consensus approach was used to determine eligibility and resolve any disagreements, with the senior author (AEZ) consulted for final determination as needed. Data collection process Two reviewers (AZ, MC) manually and systematically extracted and summarized information on study design, goals, VM description, setting, location, target population, sample, results, and limitations from each included article (see Additional file 1 ). All authors reviewed and assessed the evidence and limitations of the included articles, including strength of evidence for each included article [ 29 ]. Heterogeneity of the study designs and methods precluded data pooling and meta-analysis. Outcome measures Outcomes of primary interest fell into four main categories: (1) feasibility, (2) acceptability, (3) reach, and (4) impact. Feasibility was conceptualized as the potential for the VM to be effective within a given setting, with subconstructs of demand (number of items dispensed from the VM and patterns in VM usage), implementation (considerations for VM placement and/or the extent the proposed plan was carried through), and practicality (associated time, resources, and/or costs in implementing and/or maintaining the VM) [ 30 ]. Acceptability was defined as the attitudes and perceptions among VM users and/or stakeholders toward agreeability of VMs within a given setting, and the potential barriers and facilitators to VM-related use satisfaction [ 31 ]. Reach was assessed by the representativeness of the VM users in relation to the target population [ 32 ]. Impact was defined as the influence of the VM on community or individual-level outcomes relevant to the specific VM’s target population and/or intention [ 32 ]. Results Eligible articles-identification The multi-database search identified 2946 articles. After removing duplicates, 2461 unique articles remained, and their titles/abstracts were screened, leading to the identification of 80 potentially-eligible articles. Full text review of these 80 articles led to the exclusion of 44 articles (including one not published in English [ 33 ]), and the inclusion of 36 eligible articles. The search of references listed within these eligible articles and from prior pertinent reviews [ 14 , 25 , 26 , 34 – 36 ] yielded additional 80 original research articles. In addition, four articles [ 37 – 40 ] were identified through personal connections with harm reduction organizations. Among these additional 84 potentially-eligible articles, the screening process identified 42 duplicates, and the remaining 42 titles/abstracts were screened; of those, nine full-text articles were reviewed, and all were deemed eligible (Fig. 1 ). Overall, these above pathways yielded a total of 45 eligible articles included in this systematic review (Table 2 ).
